## Part 1 · 00:00

This shift in perspective captures the essence of Sigman Freud's critique. For millennia, organized religion has shaped civilizations, grounded moral systems, and offered meaning in the face of mortality. But for Sigman Freud, religion was not the answer to life's deepest questions. It was a problem disguised as a cure.

Rather than revealing truth, religion functioned as a collective neurosis, a shared psychological defense that shielded individuals from the harsh realities of life. While it offered comfort, Freud believed that it did so at the expense of intellectual clarity and psychological autonomy.

Freud lived in the crossroads of cultural tension and religious authority. One of Freud's most radical ideas was that the belief in God mirrors a child's relationship with their father.

[05:17] The child vulnerable and afraid idealizes the father as all powerful, all knowing and protective. As adults, Freud believed we carry that longing into religious belief. God is the idealized father, moral authority, source of comfort and punisher of wrongdoing. He argued that religious devotion is a form of prolonged childhood dependency. The gods retain the features of the father and the religious believer's relation to his god remains that of a child to his father. Freud draws a direct line between religious belief and early developmental psychology.

[05:54] In early life, the father is experienced as both protector and authority, a source of comfort, but also of fear and limitation. Freud argued that this complex relationship becomes internalized and unconsciously projected onto a divine figure in adulthood. God in this framework is not a metaphysical being but a psychological substitute, an exalted version of the father who offers security, moral guidance, and the illusion of permanence.

[07:41] Freud's theory about the psychological origins of religion begins in totem taboo where he proposes a mythic scenario to explain the early developments of moral and religious systems in what he called primitive human societies. He imagines a primal tribe dominated by a single powerful father figure who held absolute authority. The young males or sons were excluded and resentful. Eventually they banded together and killed the father in an act of rebellion. But after the murder, they are overwhelmed by guilt.

[08:19] To cope with this guilt, they begin to idealize the father they destroyed, elevating him into a sacred figure. In Freud's view, this is how the earliest forms of religion and morality emerged. The father becomes a totem, a symbolic object of worship, and the prohibition against killing him evolves into a moral law. They hated the father who presented such a powerful obstacle to their craving for power and their sexual desires. But they loved and admired him too.

[08:53] After they had got rid of him and had satisfied their hate and had carried out their wish for identification by devouring him, their love had to assert itself. This took the form of remorse. It set up the totem in the place of the father and created the common feeling of guilt which was the beginning of morality. Freud later returns to this theory in Moses and monotheism where he applies it specifically to the emergence of monotheism and the figure of Moses.

[09:23] He argues that the psychological structure behind toemic religion, the murder, guilt and symbolic restoration of the father is also at work in the formation of Jewish monotheism. In Freud's interpretation, the god of monotheism is a return of the repressed father figure, a singular moral authority who commands obedience and channels the unresolved ambivalence of the sons into structured religious worship. The act of violence was subsequently undone by remorse. The father was elevated to a god. Freud's theories on religion and belief have been the subject of sustained criticism.

[09:53] His most speculative work, particularly totem and taboo and Moses and monotheism, rests on mythologized reconstructions of early human history for which there is no anthropological evidence. The idea of a primal father murdered by a band of sons, later deified out of guilt, is not grounded in historical or archaeological data, but in psychoanalytic symbolism. Critics have also challenged his assumptions that individual psychological patterns such as the Edypus complex can be directly scaled up to explain the origins of entire religious systems.

## Part 2 · 10:29

[10:29] This move, while conceptually bold, is methodologically weak and widely regarded as reductive. That said, not all of Freud's reflections on religion are dismissed. in the future of an illusion. His argument that religious belief functions as a form of psychological wish fulfillment, providing comfort in the face of fear, helplessness, and mortality, remains influential, though still theoretical. This view has shaped modern understanding of belief, not only in religion, but in ideology and collective myth.

[11:02] In short, Freud's psychological critique of religion retains intellectual relevance, even as his historical reconstructions are broadly rejected. Religion is widely regarded as a complex phenomenon, sometimes harmful, sometimes healing. It can foster community, provide meaning, and even aid mental health. Freud too recognized that religious belief offers emotional comfort in the face of suffering, provides a sense of order and helps regulate behavior within society.

[11:37] In his view, religion was a necessary stage in human development, a way to manage fear, enforce morality and hold civilizations together before the rise of science and reason. But ultimately, Freud believed that humanity should move beyond these inherited illusions in pursuit of greater intellectual honesty and psychological maturity. For all of the positive aspects of religious belief, it's not always about truth. It's often about need. For Freud, religion was not evil, but it was dangerous because it discouraged people from confronting reality and from growing up.
